name: Gall's Law
statement: A complex system that works is invariably found to have evolved from a simple system that worked.
meaning: Working complexity grows out of working simplicity: you rarely get a big system right by designing the whole thing up front.
mechanism: A simple system that works is a foundation you can trust: you add to it one change at a time and check that each step still works. A complex system built from scratch has too many interacting parts to get right at once, and too many places for a fault to hide, so it tends not to work, and patching rarely rescues it. Evolution beats grand design because it validates continuously.

examples.text: The web began as a plain way to link documents and grew, one working feature at a time, into a platform. It is the standard illustration of the law: a complex system whose every layer was added to something that already worked.

In 'Things You Should Never Do' (2000), Joel Spolsky called a from-scratch rewrite 'the single worst strategic mistake' a software company can make, citing Netscape: rewriting the browser stalled releases for years while competitors advanced. Old code encodes hard-won fixes a blank sheet discards.

Healthcare.gov (2013) went live as a vast system wiring together many agencies and insurers at once, and collapsed for most users on launch day: a complex system built and switched on whole, rather than evolved from a working simple one.

variants.name: Worse is better
variants.text: Richard Gabriel's thesis (c. 1989–91): a simpler design that ships and spreads often beats the more correct, more complete one that arrives late. A close cousin: simplicity wins by getting into the world and evolving there.

variants.name: The MVP / incremental delivery
variants.text: The modern descendant: ship a minimal product that works, then grow it from real use. Agile and MVP practice are Gall's Law turned into method.

whyItMatters: It is an argument for starting small and iterating: ship a simple thing that works, then grow it, rather than betting that a big up-front design will survive first contact with reality. It underpins the modern preference for MVPs and incremental delivery.

working.lead: Ship a simple thing that works first
working.text: get a small end-to-end system running before you elaborate it; a working core is the foundation everything else validates against.

working.lead: Grow it one change at a time
working.text: add complexity incrementally and confirm the whole still works at each step, so a fault has nowhere to hide.
starting over from a blank sheet throws away the edge cases the working system already handles; prefer refactoring the thing that runs.

working.lead: Remember simple is necessary, not sufficient
working.text: Gall's own caveat is that 'a simple system may or may not work': starting small buys you a path, not a guarantee.

limits: Gall wrote Systemantics as satire, and the law is an aphorism, not a proven theorem. There is no study behind it. It leans on survivorship bias: we observe the complex systems that survived and infer they all grew from simple ones, without seeing the simple systems that never grew or the clean-slate designs that quietly succeeded. Clean-sheet redesign is sometimes genuinely necessary, and the strong 'never rewrite' reading is contested: documented cases exist on both sides. And Gall's own qualifier undercuts naïve optimism: a simple system may or may not work, so starting small is necessary but never sufficient.
misreadings: It does not say planning or architecture are useless, or that any simple thing will grow into the right complex thing: plenty of simple systems evolve into messes. The claim is about the reliable path to working complexity, not a guarantee about the destination.
origin: Stated by the author and paediatrician John Gall in his 1975 book General Systemantics (later retitled Systemantics, then The Systems Bible). The book pairs it with a blunt corollary: 'a complex system designed from scratch never works and cannot be patched up to make it work; you have to start over, beginning with a working simple system', and a caution that 'a simple system may or may not work'. The label 'Gall's Law' was attached by later readers, not by the book itself.

sources.text: Gall, J. (1975). General Systemantics: An Essay on How Systems Work, and Especially How They Fail. (both halves of the law at pp. 65 and 71)
Spolsky, J. (6 April 2000). "Things You Should Never Do, Part I." Joel on Software. — the Netscape from-scratch-rewrite cautionary tale.
